messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Rajesh

Rajesh was forty-nine when it happened, cleaning the lobby of a downtown office building on a Tuesday morning in March. He had been working nights at the same property for seven years—a reliable, quiet job that suited him after the divorce, after his daughter stopped calling. The work required little conversation, and he preferred it that way. That morning, as he was moving a heavy brass planter to mop behind it, one of the building's tenants, a younger man in an expensive suit, rushed past him without looking. Rajesh turned sharply, the planter still in his hands, and it caught the man across the face and shoulder as he pivoted. The man fell hard, his arm bent beneath him at an angle that made Rajesh's stomach drop. There was blood on the marble floor. An ambulance came. The man had a fractured orbital bone, a dislocated shoulder, and a concussion. Rajesh had been questioned by police, cleared of criminal negligence, but the building's management had quietly let his contract lapse three months later.

Now, three years on, Rajesh lived in a studio apartment in a neighborhood he did not choose, working irregular shifts at a hotel housekeeping service. He was fifty-two, divorced, estranged from his daughter, and marked by something he could not shake. When he closed his eyes at night, he did not see a movie of the event—he saw snapshots. The moment the planter left his hands. The man's face as he turned. The specific angle of the arm on the floor. Each image arrived fully formed, vivid and still, like photographs someone had arranged in his mind. These pictures came to him unbidden throughout the day: while he was folding sheets, while he stood in line at a bodega, while he sat alone in his apartment on a Sunday afternoon. A sudden sound—a door slamming, a sharp voice in the hallway—could trigger the entire sequence in an instant, flooding him with a rage so intense it frightened him. He would feel his fists clench, his jaw tighten, heat rising through his chest. The rage was not directed outward anymore; it had turned inward, pooling into a conviction he could not escape.

What tormented Rajesh most was not the injury he had caused, but what the injury meant about him. He had come to believe that he was fundamentally careless, reckless—a man whose nature was to destroy. He had acted in a way that contradicted everything he understood about himself. For decades, he had prided himself on being careful, methodical, a man who took pride in his work and treated others with respect. Yet in one moment, he had proven himself capable of serious harm. The snapshots that invaded his mind seemed to confirm this darker truth: he was the kind of man who hurt people. When the images arrived—the planter suspended in air, the man's shocked expression—they brought with them a crushing sense of culpability. It was his action, his carelessness, his failure to look before turning. Nothing felt meaningful anymore because he could no longer trust himself. His work, once a source of quiet dignity, now felt like a performance, a pretense that he was still a good man when the evidence suggested otherwise. He had acted against his own values, and the memory of those frozen moments kept insisting that this was who he really was.

Three months ago, Rajesh had stopped accepting extra shifts. Two months ago, he had declined his sister's invitation to his nephew's wedding. Last month, he had sat in his apartment for an entire Saturday without turning on the television, unable to concentrate on anything, feeling the weight of his own unworthiness. It was his sister who finally insisted he see someone, who found him a therapist who worked with people carrying trauma. Rajesh came to the first appointment uncertain whether he deserved help, uncertain whether anything could change the fact of what he had done. What he hoped for, though he barely admitted it to himself, was the possibility that he might be something other than the man those snapshots insisted he was.
